A1.justification: Both PDFs describe S2S-Arena. Their complete text, tables, equations, figures and appendices support comparison despite substantial revision. The original pilot results and four-level framework can be matched across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original human comparisons of six speech systems, Elo rankings, and analyses of failures, multilingual support and evaluation biases.

after.justification: v2 reports 1,001 comparisons of ten systems, automatic-judge validation, synthetic-data checks and additional performance analyses. It also retains the human pilot results in Appendix A.5.

M1.justification: The benchmark procedure gains iterative GPT-4o self-instruction with controllable speech synthesis, rating-gap-weighted model pairing, and Gemini-based automatic judging for the main evaluation. These substantially extend v1's manual construction and evaluation workflow. The change from levels L0-L3 to L1-L4 preserves their definitions.

E1.justification: The four domains persist, but v2 adds the evaluated Augment corpus and broadens task requirements. For example, natural-sound tasks extend from generation-only in v1 Table 7 to perception and joint perception/generation in v2 Table 8. The seed inventory changes from 21 to 19 categories; querying symptoms disappears from that inventory but remains in Augment Figure 4.

E2.justification: The original six-system comparison survives in v2 Table 10. The new main comparison adds evaluated systems including Doubao, GLM-4-Voice, Qwen2.5-Omni, Kimi-Audio and Mini-Omni2, and uses Qwen-backed FunAudioLLM rather than its pilot GPT-4o variant. Judge comparisons also change from GPT-4o-realtime/Qwen2-Audio to Gemini 2.5-Pro/Qwen2.5-Omni.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates 1,001 automatically judged matches on the 950-example Augment set, introduces weighted pair sampling, and expands the seed set from 154 to 293 examples. The retained human pilot is described as 432 comparisons by 19 annotators, versus approximately 400 comparisons and 22 annotators in v1; unchanged pilot scores do not establish that it was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds difficulty-specific architectural analyses, Doubao/GPT-4o and Kimi-Audio/SpeechGPT case studies, a 100-sample synthetic-data validation study, and task clustering. It removes v1's quantified failure taxonomy, targeted sarcasm and multilingual probes, and positional/length-bias investigations. Domain-level comparisons were already present in v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds a limited ranking-stability assessment using 1,000 match-level bootstrap resamples, reporting Spearman correlation of 0.94 ± 0.03, and introduces Cohen's kappa for judge agreement. Human agreement remains 83.7%, while v1's automatic-judge repeatability measurements disappear. Bootstrap resampling does not establish additional model-generation runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds overall, domain and difficulty results for the expanded comparison, including Qwen2.5-Omni's leading Elo of 1246.1, plus Gemini's 82.87% human agreement and synthetic-data validation results. These use different settings from v1. All pilot Elo values in v1 Table 4 remain unchanged in v2 Table 10; several earlier diagnostic results are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.1 adds a mathematical definition of rating-gap-dependent sampling weights, including their location and scale parameters. The Elo expectation and update equations from v1 Appendix C remain equivalent, and the renamed interaction levels introduce no new mathematical framework or proofs.

C1.justification: The central benchmark objective persists, but the headline contributions shift from a small manual evaluation and findings about cascaded systems, multilingual bottlenecks and generation failures to scalable construction, automatic evaluation, and industrial-versus-academic capability gaps. Architectural explanations and difficulty-dependent performance become central claims.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations about domain trade-offs and the influence of training data, encoders, backbones, vector quantization and decoders. These largely replace v1's multilingual and evaluation-bias explanations. New limitations address synthetic-distribution bias and short-range interactions. Architectural attributions rely on cross-model comparisons, including a flow-matching explanation involving Doubao despite its decoder being listed as unknown.

D1.justification: v2 adds generation schemas and prompts, five-shot sampling, retry/checkpoint rules, synthesis tools, task-normalization and clustering settings, and API/local execution details including an A6000 GPU. It states that inference code will be released upon acceptance. Some exact pilot component checkpoint identifiers supplied in v1 are no longer specified.

R1.justification: Related work expands to benchmarks such as Vstyle, VoxDialogue, Multivox and SpeechJudge, alongside newer speech systems and self-instruction literature. The model discussion is reorganized around encoders, backbones and decoders, with additional industry/academia positioning. These are substantive additions beyond retained works' publication and bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, construction description, results narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten and reorganized. The title and author information change, ethical considerations and acknowledgments appear, and appendices A-D become subsections A.1-A.5, incorporating the former main human evaluation.

P2.justification: The construction diagram is redrawn, the human-evaluation workflow figure disappears, and a ten-model heatmap replaces the original six-model display. Tables gain win/loss statistics and difficulty-by-architecture comparisons; dataset summaries, a task-distribution chart and boxed prompts are added. The original Elo table moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: Human-calibrated automatic judging, difficulty-specific results, bootstrap stability checks and fuller implementation details make v2 a more useful and better-supported benchmark. The gain is limited by removal of evaluation-bias tests and unsupported architectural attributions. Numerical inconsistencies also weaken the discussion: Table 4 gives Kimi-Audio 142 wins, although the prose identifies GPT-4o's 140 as the largest total. The added validation and diagnostic value support a limited net improvement.
